reference_summary: Gradient descent is the foundational optimization algorithm for training machine learning models. It minimizes a loss function by iteratively updating parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient. The learning rate controls step size: too large diverges, too small converges slowly. Variants include batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent. Momentum and adaptive optimizers such as Adam and RMSProp accelerate convergence.

Logistic regression is a classification algorithm that models the probability that an input belongs to the positive class. It passes a linear combination of features through the sigmoid function which maps real values to the range (0, 1). Training uses the binary cross-entropy loss which is convex and globally optimizable by gradient descent. Multinomial logistic regression generalizes to multiple classes via softmax. Regularization (L1 or L2) prevents overfitting.

A neural network is a layered model that learns mappings from inputs to outputs. A feed-forward network has an input layer, hidden layers, and an output layer; each layer applies a linear transformation followed by a non-linearity. Forward propagation produces predictions; backpropagation computes parameter gradients via the chain rule. Activation functions like ReLU introduce non-linearity. Dropout, batch normalization, and weight decay are common regularizers.

Generalization error is the model's error on unseen data while training error is its error on data it has seen. The gap between the two measures how well the model generalizes. Overfitting happens when a high-capacity model memorizes training data including noise; underfitting happens when capacity is too low. Detection: watch the validation loss diverge from training loss. Remedies: L1/L2 regularization, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, more data.

Model evaluation measures how well a model performs on unseen data. The simplest approach is a train-test split, typically 80/20, with stratification when class labels are imbalanced. K-fold cross validation generalizes this by training and evaluating k times so every example serves as both training and test data. Common metrics include accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and AUC. The bias-variance tradeoff describes how simple models underfit and complex ones overfit.
